messages.author: 5a05cd5293b6ec52
messages.subject: degrees of freedom path model
parts:
Hello,
could you tell me how lavaan calculates the degrees of freedom for a multigroup path model?

According to the formula ((v*(v+1))/2) I get 15 information per group; so in total 30. In the model I estimate 14 parameters (2*7) which leads to 16 degrees of freedom. According to the output the model has 4 degrees of freedom.

Thanks

Here is my code:

data(HolzingerSwineford1939)
library(lavaan)



model <- "x1 ~ x2 + x3
           x4 ~ x5 + x3"
fit <- sem(model,
           data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
           group = "school",
           meanstructure = FALSE)
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

v = 5
pars = 7*2
information = (0.5*v*(v+1))*2
information - pars

messages.subject: Re: degrees of freedom path model
parts:
Mirko,

For starters, when you're not estimating a mean structure, the correct
formula is (v*(v-1))/2. The formula you use includes sample means as
part of the original information.

That should get you closer.

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: degrees of freedom path model
parts:
Oh, you're right--I'm sorry.

Still, I'm not sure where you think you're using parameters.

x2, x3, and x5 have variances and covariances--6 parameters per group.
4 regression relations per group.
x1 and x4 residual variances--2 parameters per group.
auto.cov.y defaults to TRUE in sem()--1 parameter for x1 with x4.

That's 13 per group, times two groups is 26.

30-26=4df.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: degrees of freedom path model
parts: It seems to me that the formula (v*(v+1))/2 only refers to the input (co)variances

But in your model there are 3 exogenous covariates: x2, x3, and x5.  Treating those as fixed means that their 6 observed (co)variances are not included as input data, nor are they estimated (if they were estimated by setting fixed.x=FALSE, you would have 6 additional estimates).  So your count of observed information (per group) when treating exogenous variables as fixed is:

nExo = 3
nEndo = 2
nObs = nExo(nExo + 1)/2 + nExo*nEndo

That's 9 (co)variances per group minus 7 estimated parameters per group, leaving df=2 per group (df=4 overall).

Again, your original math would work out correctly too if you treated all variables as endogenous, but you would have to add 6 more (co)variances among the exogenous predictors to your parameter count, so it would come out to df=4 anyway.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
